title: Trace phenotype latency catalog and prioritization
body:
TL;DR:
We created a lightweight catalog of distinct trace phenotypes observed in recent production e2e latency captures and instrumented synthetic workloads. Each phenotype has representative p50/p95/p99 numbers and per-stage breakdowns (ingest, routing, tokenization, model serve, kv/cache ops, batching wait, postprocess, egress). Purpose: prioritize mitigation experiments (kernel + runtime + policy changes) by expected product impact and implementation cost.

Context and motivation:
- Multiple recent P99 regressions were surfaced by customers and SRE alerts; root causes varied (kv cache churn, unexpected batching wait, RPC retries).
- We need a repeatable way to map an incoming trace to a phenotype bucket and a playbook for short/medium-term fixes.
- This doc is an actionable catalog for on-call, incident leads, and performance owners; it is not exhaustive but focuses on high-frequency/high-impact phenotypes.

Dataset and methodology:
- Sources: sampled production traces (Jan–Nov 2025), synthetic trace captures from our workload generator (request shapes: short prompt, long prompt, multi-turn, streaming), and staging A/B experiments that toggled batching/window settings.
- Sampling: for production we used reservoir sampling at 0.1% keyed by route and model. Each trace includes per-stage timestamps and stack tags (node id, model variant, cache-key-hit/miss, seq_len, is_streaming).
- Metrics extracted: p50/p95/p99 e2e, stage medians/95/99, % of token time in model device vs kernel overhead, queue wait time quantiles.
- Labeling: traces were clustered by a simple rule engine (cache hit/miss, batch_size observed, seq_len bucket, cold-start flag). Human review for ambiguous clusters.

Phenotype catalog (representative examples):
1) Short prompt, cache-hit, single-token response ("short-cache-hit")
   - Typical request shape: user prompt ~20 tokens, model response ~10 tokens.
   - Representative e2e: p50 22 ms, p95 36 ms, p99 60 ms.
   - Stage breakdown (p95): ingest 1 ms, routing 2 ms, tokenization 1 ms, model-serve (device exec) 18 ms, kv-cache lookup 6 ms, batching-wait 3 ms, postprocess+egress 5 ms.
   - Notes: tight tail dominated by occasional cache lookup latency spikes (eg. network latency to external KVS when node probe fails).

2) Warm multi-token generation, moderate seqlen ("steady-stream")
   - Shape: prompt 40 tokens, output 120 tokens streaming.
   - Representative e2e: p50 320 ms, p95 640 ms, p99 1100 ms (streaming partial latencies observed per token).
   - Breakdown (p95, first-token vs mid-token): first-token has higher routing+initial kv load; mid-token dominated by model token time 18–26 ms/token and occasional batching wait spikes of 30–60 ms when batch windows misalign.
   - Notes: batching misalignment across routes is the largest source of p95 variability for mid-token latency.

3) Cold-start / model-warmup ("cold-quantize-warmup")
   - Shape: any request routed to a node that recently scaled up or swapped model variant.
   - e2e: p50 45 ms, p95 220 ms, p99 920 ms.
   - Breakdown (p99): image-pull / model-load operations: 450 ms, kernel init & quant table warmup 180 ms, routing 10 ms, model-serve steady 120 ms, postprocess 20 ms.
   - Mitigations: aggressive proactive prewarmed pools for critical routes; async background model load with fallback to smaller model.

4) Large prompt, long-sequence decoding ("long-seqlen-bulk")
   - Shape: prompt 600 tokens, output 800 tokens.
   - e2e: p50 6.8 s, p95 12.0 s, p99 18.5 s.
   - Breakdown (p95): tokenization & input packing 120 ms, KV/attention cache memory copy overhead 1.2 s, device model time 9.0 s, batching overhead 1.1 s (due to large KV memcpy), egress 0.5 s.
   - Notes: memory copy + KV cache maintenance scales superlinearly with seq_len; quantization choices heavily affect device-exec time.

5) Routing-induced fallback loop ("fallback-reroute-loop")
   - Shape: transient regional congestion triggers policy fallback to alternative model variant; coupled with retry logic creates loops.
   - e2e: p50 150 ms, p95 1200 ms, p99 4200 ms.
   - Breakdown (p99): initial route attempt 50 ms, retry + cold variant lead 800 ms, subsequent retries pile up causing queue delays 3300 ms.
   - Action: implement backoff + circuit breaker in routing layer; add fast-path for single retry only.

6) Batching wait dominated for low QPS routes ("micro-batch-wait")
   - Shape: low throughput but latency-sensitive routes with small outputs.
   - e2e: p50 45 ms, p95 410 ms, p99 1100 ms.
   - Breakdown (p95): batching queue wait 360 ms, model exec 20 ms, other stages 30 ms.
   - Mitigation: per-route QPS-aware dynamic batch windows; fallback to non-batched fast-path for strict latency SLAs.

Root-cause patterns and heuristics for automated classification:
- Cache-miss spikes: high kv latency correlation with external KVS timeouts; heuristic: kv_latency_p95 > 20 ms and kv_hit_rate < 85%.
- Batching-alignment spikes: observed when large fraction of requests have wide seq_len distribution; heuristic: batch_size_stddev / mean > 0.5 and batch_wait_p95 > 80 ms.
- Cold-load: node model_load_time > 200 ms within trace window.
- Routing loops: >1 external route attempt within trace and total_retries > 1.

Findings and non-obvious observations:
- Small-fraction long tails: ~0.4% of traces account for >30% of aggregate token time; many of those map to either fallback-reroute-loop or external kv latency spikes.
- Per-node variability: p99 difference across otherwise identical nodes can be 3–4x driven by local NIC interrupts and noisy neighbors on colocated control-plane tasks.
- Quantization tradeoffs: int8 builds reduce device-exec p50 by ~25% but increase p99 variance in long-seqlen cases where kernel tiling changes.
- Batching tuning: reducing max-wait from 50ms -> 20ms lowers p95 for latency-sensitive routes but increases per-token cost ~6%; worthwhile for routes with SLA tags.

Prioritization matrix (impact vs cost):
- High impact / low effort: routing backoff + single-retry circuit breaker; patching client-side KVS timeouts.
- High impact / medium effort: per-route adaptive batching windows + fast-path bypass.
- Medium impact / high effort: transparent pre-warming and prioritized model pulls across all critical routes.

Immediate recommended experiments (owners + target dates):
1) Implement routing circuit breaker prototype on staging (owner: Michael Chen) — target: 2026-03-10. Measure reduction in fallback-reroute-loop traces.
2) Per-route batch-window A/B (owner: Riley Thompson) — target: 2026-03-24. Two cohorts: default and adaptive; collect per-route p95 and cost delta.
3) KVS client tuning for network retries (owner: Priya Desai) — target: 2026-03-05. Instrument kv client metrics and test under induced packet loss.

Playbook snippets (for on-call):
- If a p99 alert fires with e2e > 2s for short routes: check trace tag cache_hit==false and kv_latency_p95 > 50 ms; escalate to infra KVS team and enable degraded-local-cache.
- If mid-token stalls show batching_wait spikes: toggle route to non-batched fast-path and schedule A/B day for adaptive windows.
- For repeated cold-loads: pin hot routes to prewarm pool and add ticket to release-engineering to prioritize smaller warm containers.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Should we instrument kernel-level metrics (GPU PCIe stalls, memcpy hotspots) in prod more broadly? cost vs signal tradeoff.
- Is there a safe default global batch-window that benefits majority without harming cost? Need more A/B slices across customers.
- Collect more labeled traces for streaming vs non-streaming separation to improve classifier accuracy.

Appendix: representative query to extract traces for a phenotype
SQL-like pseudo-query:
SELECT trace_id, e2e_ms, stage_times, tags
FROM traces
WHERE model_variant = 'redwood-1.7b'
  AND seq_len_between(5,50)
  AND kv_hit = true
  AND batch_wait_ms > 100
ORDER BY e2e_ms DESC
LIMIT 100;

Contact / owners: Asha Patel (author), Michael Chen (routing), Riley Thompson (batching experiments), Priya Desai (kv/cache).

Notes: save this as a living catalog; we'll add new phenotypes as we see them in Q2–Q3 2026.
